title: AI-Driven Closed-Loop Adaptive Execution Framework for Efficient ERP–Blockchain Integration
content:
Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems increasingly rely on blockchain technologies to provide secure, transparent, and auditable transaction processing for high-volume enterprise workloads. However, practical ERP–blockchain integration remains challenged by confirmation-latency instability, workload-dependent performance fluctuations, and excessive on-chain storage growth under dynamically varying transaction conditions.
This paper investigates an AI-driven adaptive execution framework for ERP-inspired blockchain workloads whose architecture is closed-loop by design; the evaluated pipeline implements workload prediction, rule-based execution control and hybrid-storage regulation, whereas continuous feedback collection and model retraining are proposed but not implemented or evaluated. The evaluation uses block-level Bitcoin traces from 2020 and a leakage-free experimental pipeline with strict chronological train/validation/test separation, validation-only model and threshold selection, bootstrap confidence intervals and randomization-based controls. Four findings emerge. First, block-interarrival confirmation latency at 10-minute granularity is not predictable from lagged workload history (selected model: Gradient Boosting; test R² = 0.010; RMSE improvement over the training mean = 0.54%). Second, near-term workload intensity is predictable: with the elapsed time since the last block as an additional real-time predictor, test R² reached 0.430 for transactions per block and 0.475 for block-fill ratio, with RMSE 30.6% and 30.1% lower than a persistence forecast. Third, in a mechanism-based queue simulation of ERP-record anchoring, batching ERP records reduced fee cost by about 98% relative to immediate submission at a 2-hour latency SLA; however, at the default setting every adaptive policy cost 42.7% more than the best static periodic policy, and a machine-learning congestion forecast gave no measurable advantage over a reactive rule or batching by age alone. Fourth, a trace-driven hybrid-storage estimate shows a 40.1% net reduction in on-chain footprint under an assumed fixed 70%/30% allocation policy, with an estimated mean retrieval latency of 6.87 ms versus 2.0 ms for all-on-chain storage; these are simulation estimates under declared assumptions, not physical measurements.
A rule-based adaptive controller, whose thresholds were optimized by grid search on the validation partition only under a hard activation-rate cap (≤ 50%), achieved a limited improvement over a static baseline in simulation (MAE 3.22%, RMSE 4.26%, confirmation-latency variance 7.03%; 95% bootstrap CI for the MAE improvement: [2.96%, 3.49%]). An activation-matched randomization control shows, however, that 84% of this MAE gain is reproduced when the same actions are placed on randomly chosen windows, indicating that the improvement reflects how often the controller acts more than the accuracy of its targeting. The controller effects rely on assumed action coefficients and are not measured deployment effects.
These results argue for evaluating AI-driven blockchain execution frameworks against explicit naive and randomized baselines before attributing performance gains to predictive intelligence. The workload-intensity prediction result, the mechanism-based queue-simulation methodology, and the validation protocol — including the randomization-based control — constitute the primary contributions of this work.
